Error
AIR-er
n.
From Latin error, a wandering, from errare, to stray. Webster 1828: a wandering from the truth; a mistake in judgment; also, a deviation from law or right. The Latin picture is exact for the biblical use: error is not chiefly a wrong idea but a wrong road, and the New Testament speaks of the error of his way.

Biblical Definition

Scripture treats error as something a man walks in and can be turned out of. James gives the classic statement: he which converteth the sinner from the error of his way shall save a soul from death, and shall hide a multitude of sins (James 5:20) — a wandering, a turning back, a soul saved. Jude names three errors by the men who ran in them: the way of Cain… the error of Balaam for reward… the gainsaying of Core (Jude 11), so that error has a genealogy and can be identified by its ancestors. Peter warns believers to beware lest ye also, being led away with the error of the wicked, fall from your own stedfastness (2 Peter 3:17), and John draws the sharpest line in the New Testament between two spirits: Hereby know we the spirit of truth, and the spirit of error (1 John 4:6). The Old Testament shows the seriousness. Uzzah reached out to steady the ark and God smote him there for his error; and there he died by the ark of God (2 Samuel 6:7). Ecclesiastes forbids the excuse: neither say thou before the angel, that it was an error (Ecclesiastes 5:6). Sincerity is not a defence in the presence of God; it is the reason a Mediator is necessary.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines ERROR as a wandering or deviation from the truth; a mistake in judgment by which men assent to what is not true; and also a deviation from law, right, or duty — a sin or transgression.

expand to see more

ERROR, n. [L. error, from erro, to wander.] — A wandering or deviation from the truth; a mistake in judgment, by which men assent to or believe what is not true.

A mistake made in writing or other performance; an inaccuracy.

A wandering from the path of duty or rectitude; a deviation from law or right; sin; transgression.

Webster’s third sense is the biblical one and it is the one modern English has nearly lost. In Scripture an error is not merely something a man thinks; it is something he does, and repents of.

Key Scripture

2 Samuel 6:7 — "And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Uzzah; and God smote him there for his error; and there he died by the ark of God."

Ecclesiastes 5:6 — "Suffer not thy mouth to cause thy flesh to sin; neither say thou before the angel, that it was an error: wherefore should God be angry at thy voice, and destroy the work of thine hands?"

James 5:20 — "Let him know, that he which converteth the sinner from the error of his way shall save a soul from death, and shall hide a multitude of sins."

2 Peter 3:17 — "Ye therefore, beloved, seeing ye know these things before, beware lest ye also, being led away with the error of the wicked, fall from your own stedfastness."

1 John 4:6 — "We are of God: he that knoweth God heareth us; he that is not of God heareth not us. Hereby know we the spirit of truth, and the spirit of error."

Modern Corruption

Error is corrupted when doctrinal wandering is reclassified as diversity of perspective, so that 1 John 4:6’s two spirits become two traditions, and when sincerity is accepted as a defence that Ecclesiastes 5:6 explicitly refuses.

expand to see more

1 John 4:6 recognizes exactly two spirits, the spirit of truth and the spirit of error, and it gives a test: whether a man hears the apostolic word. That binary is intolerable to the assumption that every position is a partial view of a whole no one possesses. But the apostle is not describing temperaments; he has just required that every spirit be tried by its confession of Christ come in the flesh. Error in the New Testament is a definable thing with named practitioners — Hymenaeus and Philetus, whose word ate as a canker, Balaam, Core — and the church’s duty is to identify it and turn men from it, which is the ministry James 5:20 describes as saving a soul from death.

Uzzah and Ecclesiastes 5:6 together destroy the modern defence of sincerity. Uzzah’s intention was to protect the ark; his error was that he touched what God had said must be carried by Levites on staves, and the record does not soften the outcome. Ecclesiastes then forbids the plea outright: do not say before the angel that it was an error. This is not a portrait of a God looking for occasions to strike, but of a God whose holiness is real and whose commands about His own worship are not advisory. The remedy Scripture provides is not a lower standard but a Mediator, and it is the same book that tells us the sacrifice for sins of ignorance was appointed before Uzzah was born.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew words are from roots meaning to go astray or to err inadvertently; the Greek plane means a wandering, and it gives English planet, the wandering star.

expand to see more

Hebrew shal or shegagah (H7684) — inadvertence, error; the category of sin committed unwittingly (2 Samuel 6:7; Ecclesiastes 5:6).

Hebrew ta'ah (H8582) — to wander, to go astray; the picture behind straying from the way.

Greek plane (G4106) — a wandering, a straying; the error of his way (James 5:20), the error of Balaam (Jude 11), the spirit of error (1 John 4:6).

Greek planetes — a wanderer; Jude 13 calls false teachers wandering stars, from the same root.

Greek agnoema (G51) — a sin of ignorance; the high priest offered for the errors of the people (Hebrews 9:7).

Usage

"God smote him there for his error (2 Samuel 6:7) — good intention is not a defence where God has commanded a manner."

"The error of his way (James 5:20) — error is a road walked, and a man can be turned from it."

"The spirit of truth, and the spirit of error (1 John 4:6) — two spirits, not a spectrum, and a test to tell them apart."
